name: Prize crossword No 22,183
preamble: This Easter special is a double grid. Araucaria's special instructions are as follows: The assemblages of some birds and beasts have special names, such as a murder of crows or a fesnyng of ferrets. There are many such names in puzzle A and many birds and beasts (that may be so assembled) in puzzle B. All (unlike my ferrets) are given in Chambers. Numbers used in cross-references always apply to the OTHER puzzle.

clue.text: 23s, etc at heart

definitions.note: 23 in the other puzzle names an animal (badgers) whose assemblage is the answer

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so only the inner letters of the expanded abbreviation are kept

blocks.note: etc is short for et cetera, written out as one word of eight letters; its central four are kept

explanation.surface: A list of animals tailing off with an 'and so on' in the middle of things.
explanation.walkthrough: Expand etc to ETCETERA and keep its middle four letters. A cete is the Chambers name for a company of badgers, the other puzzle's 23.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers lists cete as the collective term for a group of badgers, which is what the other puzzle's 23 across or down supplies.

clue.text: There's tension here, but it's early days

blocks.note: first meaning: a coiled metal device that stores tension
second meaning: the season when the year is young

explanation.surface: Someone notes a strained atmosphere but reassures that things are only beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: Both definitions are phrased as places or times, with 'here' and 'it's' standing for the answer. A spring of teal is also an assemblage name in Chambers.
explanation.definitionFit: A coiled spring holds mechanical tension, and spring is the opening season of the calendar year, when growth first starts.

clue.text: Preset reminder holds little weight

indicators.note: one thing that holds another keeps it inside, so the first word wraps around the second

blocks.note: a prod is a nudge or reminder
a gramme is a tiny unit of weight

explanation.surface: A preset alarm or memo that carries only a little heft.
explanation.walkthrough: Gramme is the British spelling of gram; 'reminder' here is a nudge rather than a note.
explanation.definitionFit: Something programmed has been set up in advance to behave a certain way, just like a preset device or setting.

clue.text: It could be people that hear a horse in a storm

definitions.note: the answer is a group noun, and a crowd of humans can be called by it

indicators.note: hearing points to what is said aloud, so the horse word is taken by its sound
one item placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: gee-gee is a childish word for a horse, which sounds like two letter Gs
a gale is a strong storm wind

explanation.surface: Bystanders who hear a horse neighing in the middle of a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: Gee-gee is nursery talk for a horse. The answer is normally a flock of geese, but is also used of a noisy group of people.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaggle, properly a flock of geese, is used informally for a disorderly cluster of persons, such as a gaggle of tourists.

clue.text: Rudolf as comic relief?

blocks.note: surface reading: the reindeer with the shining nose from the Christmas song
setter's reading: Comic Relief is the British charity whose fundraising day has people wearing a plastic clown nose of that colour

explanation.walkthrough: Comic Relief is a UK charity telethon whose emblem is a clown nose. Rudolph the reindeer and charity supporters alike are described by the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Rudolph's famous glowing nose is that colour, and Comic Relief's charity day has donors wearing a matching clown nose.

clue.text: 2s upset Scottish burgh

definitions.note: 2 in the other puzzle names a bird (pheasants) whose brood is the answer

indicators.note: in a down entry something upset is turned upside down, so the word reads from the bottom

blocks.note: short for Edinburgh, the Scottish capital, a burgh itself

explanation.surface: A flock of birds overturned in a Scottish town.
explanation.walkthrough: A nide is the Chambers name for a brood of pheasants. Edin, also a poetic name for the city, comes from Edinburgh with its burgh removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers gives nide as the term for a nest or brood of pheasants, the creature supplied by the other puzzle's clue 2.

clue.text: Structure for rooks

definitions.note: the assemblage word used for a group of rooks

blocks.note: first meaning: a constructed edifice
second meaning: the collective term for a gathering of rooks

explanation.surface: Somewhere for crows to nest, or a castle tower on a chessboard.
explanation.walkthrough: Rooks look like chess pieces or nesting birds; they are birds, and Chambers gives the answer as their collective noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An edifice such as a house is a building, and Chambers records building as the special name for a flock of rooks.

clue.text: 12s or 26 downs - I'm out to be a clinger

definitions.note: 12 and 26 down in the other puzzle are birds (quails and larks) that gather in the answer

indicators.note: 'I'm out' says the single letter I leaves the phrase that follows

blocks.note: the letter I, which is out, removed from the rest
taken as written
ivy is a plant that clings to walls

explanation.surface: Someone declining to be a hanger-on in a crowd of birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm out' tells you to remove the letter I from BE IVY, leaving BEVY.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers gives bevy as the collective for quails and larks, the birds named at 12 and 26 down in the companion puzzle.

clue.text: What Bowdler did abroad - back street entrance about ten pence

indicators.note: going back means reading the foreign street word from its end
about means surrounding, so the reversed street goes round the money

blocks.note: rue is French for street, so a street abroad
X is the Roman numeral ten
p is the abbreviation for pence
a gate is an entrance

explanation.surface: Censoring a book abroad in some back-street entrance for ten pence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' tells you the street is a foreign word. Thomas Bowdler published a Shakespeare with the rude bits cut, giving us 'bowdlerise'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bowdler censored Shakespeare by cutting offensive passages, which is exactly to purge a text of objectionable material.

clue.text: Employed in treating sinuses

indicators.note: the answer is found within the word being treated, sitting inside it

blocks.note: the letters run inside this word, without its outer s's

explanation.surface: A doctor's instrument used while treating a patient's blocked sinuses.
explanation.definitionFit: Something employed is currently being used, so the phrase describes an object put to work at present.

clue.text: English plovers in Dallas

definitions.note: the family surname of the main characters in the TV soap Dallas

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
Chambers gives wing as the assemblage name for plovers

explanation.surface: English shore birds turning up in a Texan city.
explanation.walkthrough: Dallas is the American TV soap about the Ewing oil family, JR and Bobby among them.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ewings are the oil-rich Texan family at the centre of the long-running American soap opera set around that city.

clue.text: News on TV, including point presented in a refined manner

indicators.note: a word including another holds it within its letters

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information
telly is British slang for television
E for east, a compass point

explanation.surface: A news item on television delivered in a polite, posh style.
explanation.walkthrough: The point goes inside the TV word, not the news word. Gen and telly are both everyday British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Genteel means polite and refined, so acting genteelly is behaving with elegant, well-bred manners.

clue.text: Cases of witticism in a sledge

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: a gag is a joke
a luge is a small racing toboggan

explanation.surface: Instances of a joke being made on a toboggan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cases' looks like examples but means suitcases.
explanation.definitionFit: Luggage is the collective word for travellers' suitcases and bags, so cases are a typical part of it.

clue.text: Range needed for destroyer to drop first torpedo

indicators.note: dropping something lets it go, so a letter is taken away
first points to the opening letter only of the following word

blocks.note: locusts are insects that destroy crops
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A warship needing range so it can release its first torpedo.
explanation.walkthrough: Destroyer looks naval with the torpedo, but it is the crop-eating insect, which drops its T.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry a locus is the set of points satisfying a condition, and more loosely an area or range where something occurs.

clue.text: Man, maybe, that's in glasses

indicators.note: something in another is held within it

blocks.note: i.e. stands for 'that is'
specs is short for spectacles

explanation.surface: A bespectacled man is described as someone in glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' marks man as one example of the answer: humans are one kind among many.
explanation.definitionFit: Humankind is one example of a species, a biological category of organisms that can interbreed.

clue.text: Tax on ale, it may be  for  26 downs

definitions.note: 26 down in the other puzzle is larks; the answer is the name for a flock of them

indicators.note: the letters may become something else, signalling that they are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters are used as written

explanation.surface: Raising duty on beer may be welcomed by some birds.
explanation.walkthrough: An exaltation of larks is one of the best-known collective nouns.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers lists exaltation as the assemblage name for larks, the birds supplied by the other puzzle's 26 down.

clue.text: Investment in herons

definitions.note: the answer is the name for a group of these birds

blocks.note: first meaning: the military blockade of a town, an old sense of investment
second meaning: the assemblage name for herons

explanation.surface: Putting money into wading birds as a financial venture.
explanation.walkthrough: Investment here is the military sense of surrounding a town, not finance.
explanation.definitionFit: To invest a town is to besiege it, and Chambers gives siege as the special collective for a group of herons.

clue.text: 27s work like one?

definitions.note: 27 in the other puzzle is goldfinches; the answer names a flock of them
the idiom 'work like a ___', with 'one' standing for the answer

blocks.note: first meaning: the collective term for a flock of finches
second meaning: the idiom for something working perfectly

explanation.surface: Asking whether a set of birds would work as one.
explanation.walkthrough: Something that works like a charm is spectacularly effective; a charm of goldfinches is the Chambers assemblage.
explanation.definitionFit: A charm is the collective for goldfinches, and the saying about working like a magic spell means succeeding perfectly.

clue.text: Flattered by removal of prefix three times from the impure

indicators.note: removing something takes it out, so the prefix is cut away

blocks.note: ter- is the Latin prefix meaning thrice
adulterated food or drink is made impure

explanation.surface: Someone pleased at being purified of an awkward triple prefix.
explanation.walkthrough: Take TER out of ADULTERATED to leave ADULATED.
explanation.definitionFit: To adulate someone is to praise them excessively, so an adulated person has been flattered with lavish admiration.

clue.text: 3s for the first part of 13 across

definitions.note: 3 in the other puzzle is whales; the answer names a school of them
the opening letters of the other puzzle's 13 across

blocks.note: first meaning: the collective term for whales or seals
second meaning: the opening chunk of the other grid's 13 across

explanation.walkthrough: Both definitions rest on the other puzzle: its 3 is a creature that gathers in pods, and its 13 across begins with these three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A pod is the standard collective for whales, dolphins or seals, the animals named by the other puzzle's 3.

clue.text: Hobbies, etc mean turning up the right clothes

indicators.note: turning a word round makes it read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right
suits are sets of clothes

explanation.surface: Leisure interests require turning up in the correct outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning up' reads as arriving, but up is the word turned. 'Mean' is a linking 'equals', not stingy.
explanation.definitionFit: Pursuits are activities one follows for pleasure or profit, and hobbies are typical leisure examples of them.

clue.text: 28, the English point of view

definitions.note: 28 in the other puzzle is evidently fish, used here as a verb
an Angle is one of the people who gave England its name

blocks.note: first meaning: to fish with a rod and line
second meaning: one of the Germanic settlers who gave England its name
third meaning: a way of looking at things

explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings: to fish with rod and line, one of the Angles who settled England, and a perspective.
explanation.definitionFit: To angle is to fish, the Angles were early settlers whose name became England, and an angle is a slant or perspective.

clue.text: More reliable, hence supporting?

blocks.note: so, like hence, means therefore
what supports something is under it

explanation.surface: Something proves more dependable because it gives support.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is also the Chambers name for a herd of wild swine.
explanation.definitionFit: A sounder argument or structure is firmer and more trustworthy, so it is more reliable.

clue.text: Macbeth surprised about Cawdor is a gas

blocks.note: what Macbeth calls himself
Macbeth is hailed as Thane of Cawdor by the witches

explanation.surface: Macbeth taken aback by a prophecy about Cawdor, joked as hot air.
explanation.walkthrough: When the witches hail him Thane of Cawdor, a surprised Macbeth might say 'Me, thane?', which gives ME THANE.
explanation.definitionFit: Methane is a colourless flammable hydrocarbon gas, the main component of natural gas.

clue.text: Does the Queen have to pass it?

definitions.note: in the idiom 'pass ___', with 'it' standing for the answer

blocks.note: must means have to
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: Wondering whether even the monarch must meet the required standard.
explanation.walkthrough: The question reads as 'must ER?': MUST then ER. To pass muster is to meet an inspection; a muster of peacocks is the Chambers collective.
explanation.definitionFit: A muster is a military assembly for inspection, and passing it means being found acceptable, the thing you pass in that idiom.

clue.text: He had an affair, naughtiness aroused by Venus?

indicators.note: roused up suggests rising, and in a down entry a word read upwards is turned round

blocks.note: an ado is a fuss or business, an affair
sin is wrongdoing

explanation.surface: A man's illicit romance and naughtiness stirred up by the goddess of love.
explanation.walkthrough: ADO then SIN read upwards as NIS. The whole clue alludes to the myth: Adonis was Venus's beloved, so 'by Venus' completes the picture rather than the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Adonis is the beautiful youth of Greek myth loved by Venus, so he is the man who had an affair with her.

clue.text: The noises you can hear are being dropped

indicators.note: what you can hear is spoken aloud, so the answer sounds like the phrase that follows

blocks.note: dropping a clanger is British slang for making a blunder, so clangers are things dropped

explanation.surface: Audible din from things falling to the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: To drop a clanger is British slang for making an embarrassing mistake, so clangers are what get dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Clangour is a loud ringing metallic din, so its plural names several resounding noises.

clue.text: Those 22s throw to 28

definitions.note: 22 in the other puzzle is hawks; the answer names a pair or flight of them
28 in the other puzzle is evidently fish: to throw a line to fish

blocks.note: first meaning: the collective for hawks released together
second meaning: to throw a fishing line out

explanation.walkthrough: Both meanings depend on the other grid: a cast of hawks, and an angler throwing a line towards fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers names a set of hawks flown together a cast, and to cast is to throw a line or net for fish.

clue.text: Go with the crowd

blocks.note: first meaning: Scots and dialect verb meaning to walk or go
second meaning: a group or band of people

explanation.surface: Advice to conform and follow everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase looks like advice to conform; gang is an old Scots verb meaning to go, as in 'gang awa'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots, to gang is to go, and a gang is a band of people moving together, a crowd.

clue.text: Monkeys don't have a good time, quite the reverse

indicators.note: the reverse of something is its backward form, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: not having a good one means having a poor one
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Primates are miserable, or perhaps having fun after all.
explanation.walkthrough: A poor time is POOR T, which reversed gives TROOP. A troop is the collective for monkeys.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of monkeys or apes is called a troop, so the plural creatures define the collective.

clue.text: 1s prepare to travel

definitions.note: 1 in the other puzzle is a beast that runs in groups, hounds or wolves

blocks.note: first meaning: the collective term for hounds or wolves
second meaning: to put belongings into bags

explanation.surface: Some unnamed group gets ready for a trip.
explanation.definitionFit: Hounds and wolves hunt in a pack, and to pack is to fill cases before a journey.

clue.text: Hide concealing the end of the yarn

indicators.note: concealing something hides it within, so one piece goes inside the other
the end of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: an animal's hide is its skin
its final letter

explanation.surface: An animal pelt with the tail of a thread hidden in it.
explanation.walkthrough: E goes inside SKIN: SK-E-IN. Yarn looks like a story but is wool; a skein is also a flight of geese.
explanation.definitionFit: A skein is a loosely coiled length of wool or thread, so it is a quantity of yarn.

clue.text: Signs show all those loveless creatures, acid freaks

indicators.note: love is zero in tennis, a round letter, and being without it means that letter goes
something that freaks out goes wild, so these letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the definite article, pointing at every one of a set
a zoo is a collection of creatures
taken as written

explanation.surface: Animals shown off at a menagerie, with drug users acting strangely.
explanation.walkthrough: THE ZOO loses one O (love), then ACID rearranged gives DIAC.
explanation.definitionFit: The twelve signs of astrology together make up the zodiac, so the signs collectively form it.
